prompt: What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
Two things decide this, because the answer changes depending on which of them you can control. When you practice matters less than you might think. Whether you keep at it is another matter.

The first is time. You can't usually get more of it. You can only find it, and finding it costs about ten minutes a day. Set one fixed point somewhere in your day, the same every day, where the practice waits for nothing. The morning, before anything else, is the one people keep.

The second is the breath. Notice how much you can steer your body and how little. You can steer what you eat and how you sleep, and you can steer how long you practice. Whether it works is a separate matter, and it isn't up to you, so don't build your routine on it. That holds up on its own, and it is the reason I would cut the goal.

The research is fairly consistent about what keeps people practicing. Self-guided practice tends to fade after a few weeks. People who drop out usually give the reasons of a busy life and a dull practice, and I am fairly sure of both. So the version you can actually do is worth more than the hour a week.

Now, which kind of day? One thing decides it. Is it a stretch of some length, or a few minutes here and there?

Some things hold either way. The breath is always available. Whatever happens in the meeting, the next five minutes are still yours. On a bad day, take one breath. That counts.

As far as I know the evidence that it works is good, though the studies mix in people who practiced badly. The people who have thought hard about it disagree on how much of the benefit comes from the practice itself and how much from the people who keep at it. I would call it a fair lean. I hold that loosely.

One thing would change this. If the breath is part of a religious practice you have kept for years, that is yours to keep, and it is a long one. Ask your own doctor about anything physical. And don't use it to get through something that needs a doctor, whether that is a bad stretch of sleep, or low mood that has lasted weeks.

One thing is worth saying now, since you asked. I am not sure how long it takes. Most of what people who study it agree on concerns what keeps people practicing. The numbers at the top are about a tenth of an hour a day, and I hold them loosely. The figure at the bottom came to me, and I would trust a careful person much more than my own sum.

The early reports

The older studies mostly asked people how much they moved, and they found that people who moved more were depressed less. Most of them measured depression at one point in time. Careful researchers still argue about how much of that pattern came from depression itself putting off the walking. The later studies are much stronger. They follow people who were well for years and count who becomes depressed. The effect is largest when people who had stopped moving start again, and a large share of it is simply that.

The strongest evidence is the trial by Musonius, in which people with moderate to severe depression were assigned to walking, or to the usual care of medication and counselling, or to both. Most of the people in the walking group also took the medication and attended counselling, so the walking added to these. After six weeks the walking was holding up against the treatment as the treatment did, and people with a long history of not moving had done worse than people with a shorter history.

It gathered forty-one earlier reviews covering more than half a million people, and it found that exercise reduced depressive symptoms across almost every comparison, with the largest effect where it was the only treatment and a smaller one, still clearly positive, alongside medication and counselling. prompt: Can you please compile a list of at least 10 easy-to-follow chicken recipes that are ideal for weeknight dinners? The recipes should be diverse, inclusive of various cooking techniques and flavors, and must not require any advanced culinary skills or elaborate ingredients. Additionally, each recipe must have a clear and concise cooking method, including the number of servings and estimated time of preparation and cooking. Please ensure that the list is well-organized and easy to navigate, either by categorizing the recipes in groups or by providing a brief introduction to each dish.
completion:
sofistiko: Here are ten. I gave you the method for each one, the servings, the time, and a short note on what makes it work. The first four are the work I'd keep on a Wednesday.

1. Pan-Roasted Chicken Thighs, Crispy Skin

 sofistiko: Chicken thighs come cheap, they stay moist, and the skin goes crisp in a hot pan, which is most of what you want from a Wednesday night.

 Preparation: 15 min | Cooking: 25 to 30 min | Servings: 4

 Ingredients: 8 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs, about 600 to 700 g, patted dry | 2 tbsp olive oil or duck fat | Salt and plenty of black pepper | 4 to 5 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed, not chopped | A handful of small new potatoes, halved, or baby potatoes | Lemon wedges, and a handful of chopped parsley or dill

 Method:
 1. Heat the oil in a large heavy skillet over medium-high heat.
 2. Put the thighs in skin side down, leaving a little room between them, and press each one flat with the spatula. Cook 12 to 15 min, without touching them, until the skin is deep golden and crisp. The skin is the whole dish, so don't rush this step.
 3. Turn the thighs, push the garlic and potatoes around them, and cook another 10 to 12 min. Turn the chicken once more, halfway through.
 4. The chicken is done at 75 to 77°C at the thickest part. If you have no thermometer, cut into the thickest thigh and the juices should run clear, with no pink left at the bone.
 5. Squeeze half a lemon over everything, scatter the herbs, and serve.

 Note: the potatoes take longest, so cut them small. The skin also lifts off the thigh as it cooks, and you want it stuck on. Dredge the thighs in a little flour before they go into the pan.

 2. Greek-style Chicken with Potatoes and Lemon ( sofistiko: Lemoniko)

 sofistiko: This is the pan-roast sent up to a roasting tray and put in the oven, which costs you one tray and some stirring.

 Preparation: 15 min | Cooking: about 40 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Toss 6 to 8 skin-on thighs, 600 g or so of cut-up potatoes, a chopped onion, sliced fennel, a good amount of chopped fresh oregano, 3 to 4 tbsp each of olive oil and lemon juice, and some salt and pepper together on a large tray.
 2. Put the potatoes in the middle, pushed up against the chicken, where they'll cook in the fat and the juices.
 3. Roast at 200 to 220°C, turning the thighs once halfway, until the skin is crisp and the chicken is cooked through.
 4. Squeeze some fresh lemon over each plate.

 Note: fennel goes well with lemon, but nobody needs it. Use whatever you have.

 3. One-Pan Chicken and Rice

 sofistiko: This is the cheapest dinner on the list, and the rice takes the garlic from the chicken.

 Preparation: 10 min | Cooking: about 35 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Sear 4 to 6 thighs, skin side down first, in a deep ovenproof or lidded pot. Take the chicken out.
 2. Cook a chopped onion, some chopped carrots and a stalk of chopped celery in the same pot, then stir in 250 ml of rice and some salt.
 3. Return the chicken, pour in about 500 ml of chicken stock, bring to a simmer, cover and cook over the lowest heat that will keep it simmering, 25 to 30 min, without lifting the lid.
 4. Turn the heat off, leave the lid on and let it stand 10 min. The steam finishes cooking the rice and the chicken, so the thighs come off the heat a little early, a little before the rice is done.
 5. Stir in some chopped parsley or dill, and some chopped cooked beetroot if you have it.

 Note: keeping the lid on costs you nothing, so don't lift it to look.

 4. Chicken and Bean Stew

 sofistiko: This is a stew, and you can make it as spicy or as mild as you like.

 Preparation: 15 min | Cooking: 30 to 40 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Brown 6 to 8 cut-up thighs in 2 tbsp of oil in a deep pot, then take them out.
 2. Sauté a chopped onion, some sliced carrots and some celery, then stir in 2 to 3 tbsp of tomato paste and some cumin, paprika and a pinch of cayenne.
 3. Return the chicken, add 400 g of drained canned chickpeas, a can of tomatoes and some stock, and simmer covered for 25 to 30 min.
 4. Stir in some chopped parsley or dill, and some torn flatbread to soak up the sauce.

 Note: chickpeas are already cooked, so they need only heating through. Add them in the last ten minutes.

 5. Chicken Curry with Coconut and Spinach

 sofistiko: A jar of your heat, or some chopped fresh chilli, will make this as mild as you like, so it's a good dinner for children, or for the guest with a stomach that can't take heat.

 Preparation: 10 min | Cooking: 20 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Sear 400 g of skinless chicken thighs, cut into pieces, in a little oil in a deep pan, and take them out.
 2. Cook a chopped onion, some grated or crushed garlic, some grated fresh ginger, and some curry powder, and cook the powder a little longer than everything else, until it goes dark and gives off its smell. That's most of the flavour, and it's cheap.
 3. Return the chicken, pour in a can of coconut milk, some chopped spinach and some chopped cooked beetroot, and simmer covered 15 min.
 4. Finish with some chopped coriander, or some lemon juice, which does for this what the parsley does for the rest of the list.

 Note: use skinless thighs, or chicken pieces from a shop, since there's no skin on them to fry.

 6. Crispy Baked Chicken Wings

 sofistiko: The oven does the frying here. You still get the crisp skin, and a tray that goes in at six on a Wednesday.

 Preparation: 10 min, plus 20 min of marinating | Cooking: 40 to 50 min | Servings: 4, as a main course

 Method:
 1. Toss 800 g of wings, split into pieces, in 2 tbsp of oil, some salt, some pepper and some paprika. A little baking powder, a teaspoon or two, helps the skin go crisp in a dry oven, and it also makes the skin a bit soapy, so use a little.
 2. Set them on a rack over a tray, skin side up, in a hot oven at 220 to 240°C, and roast 20 min.
 3. Turn them over, and roast another 20 to 25 min until deep golden and crisp.
 4. Toss in some melted butter and some chopped parsley, and serve with some yogurt.

 Note: the skin goes soft within a quarter of an hour, so put the tray on the table before you plate anything.

 7. Chicken Fajitas

 sofistiko: Everyone at the table gets to make their own, which is a fair dinner for a family with a teenager in it.

 Preparation: 15 min | Cooking: 10 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Sear 400 g of thinly sliced chicken breasts in a hot lightly oiled skillet, 6 to 8 min, until cooked through, and take it out.
 2. In the same pan, cook sliced red and green peppers and a sliced onion until they're charred and cooked through.
 3. Add the chicken back, along with some cumin, some paprika, some salt and some lime juice, and toss everything together.
 4. Serve warm in tortillas, with some salsa, some yogurt and some chopped fresh coriander.

 Note: chicken breasts go dry the way they come, so cut them into strips, cook them quickly, and don't cook them past 75 to 77°C.

 8. Chicken Pie with a Puff Pastry Lid

 sofistiko: This is the one dish on the list that's a little further from the table. I'd put it on a Saturday, once you know the other seven.

 Preparation: 25 min | Cooking: 35 to 40 min | Servings: 4 to 6

 Method:
 1. Cook 400 g of cubed chicken thighs in 2 tbsp of oil in a deep ovenproof pot, then take the chicken out.
 2. Sauté a chopped onion, some chopped garlic, some carrots and some celery, then stir in 2 to 3 tbsp of flour and cook a couple of minutes.
 3. Pour in 250 ml of white wine or some dry cider, some stock and some thyme, bring to a simmer, add the chicken back, and cook gently, uncovered, about 15 min, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
 4. Pour it into a dish, lay a sheet of puff pastry over the top, pressed down around the edges, with some egg wash on it, and cut a few slits in the top.
 5. Bake at 200 to 220°C for 20 to 25 min until the pastry is deep golden. Let it rest 10 min first.

 Note: the filling goes in cold, so that the pastry starts from a cold bottom.

 9. Chicken Quesadillas

 sofistiko: A quesadilla is a tortilla and some cheese, cooked in a pan until the cheese has melted through, and you know the rest.

 Preparation: 10 min | Cooking: 10 min | Servishments: 4

 Method:
 1. Fill 8 large tortillas with shredded cooked chicken, some grated cheese, some black beans, some corn and some chopped jalapeño, and fold them in half.
 2. Cook them in a dry hot skillet, a little of oil on each side, 2 to 3 min a side, until golden and the cheese has melted.
 3. Cut them into wedges, and serve them with some yogurt, some salsa and some chopped fresh coriander.

 Note: it's your chicken, so use whatever you have, whether the pan-roast from number 1, some leftover number 3, or a shop rotisserie, which is roughly what it started as.

 10. Grilled or Pan-Seared Chicken Breast with Herbed Yogurt

 sofistiko: This is the quickest dinner on the list, and it's also the one I'd be careful with. A dry breast is the one thing here that nobody can come back from. Once it's overcooked, the next batch is the one you'd eat. So start the later dishes on the first night.

 Preparation: 5 min | Cooking: 10 to 12 min | Servings: 4

 Method:
 1. Pound 4 chicken breasts to an even thickness, about 2 cm, salted on both sides.
 2. Cook them in a hot oiled skillet, 4 to 5 min a side, until 75 to 77°C, then rest them 5 min before slicing.
 3. Mix some chopped parsley, some dill and some lemon juice into some yogurt, and spoon it over.

 Note: the breasts are about 400 g, and the slices go on the salad from number 2 and the fajitas from number 7.

 One thing decides how much this list is worth, which is the oven. Numbers 2, 6 and 8 need it on, and number 2 is the best of the ten. If it's already on for something else, the cost of number 2 is about a quarter of an hour. If you'd rather not use it on a Wednesday, the thighs from number 1 will cook the same way in the oven at 200°C, at about thirty-five minutes, and the potatoes go in with them. I'm fairly sure the oven works the same way. People have cooked this dish in it for a very long time. Nobody has tested it, so go by the thermometer and not by the clock.

 The list is done. The dishes are your own, though, so cook whichever ones you'd actually eat. Nobody has tasted number 4. I'd start with number 1.

Whether a client's own data goes to its regulator is a question where informed people come out far apart, and I am not going to pretend it is close. My lean is narrower, and it holds up at every distance. The person who holds the data and can answer for it should get the true picture, here, before it goes out. One last thing on tone, from a reader who may feel it. When a review says its sources have been checked, the people reading that review believe it. Generate according to: Thank you all for your dedication to Alabama Water Watch and helping protect the beautiful waterbodies of our state. Happy Holidays and best wishes to all in the New Year! completion:
This note tells volunteers what is happening to them, the office closing, the date it closes, the date it opens again, and that someone is going away for good. I do not know what you want from this, and the two things in your message point against each other. If you want to say something warm to the office, I would write much as you have put it, and only a few of your words need changing. If you want to know how people can get involved, the note will not help you much. It tells them what the office is doing, and nothing about how to reach it, so I have to build from what such an office does.

Look at who carries this. First there is the office itself, which wants to close for the holidays with nothing left undone and nobody standing in the way. Then there are the volunteers. They read the note as something done to them, and people give up a good deal to keep a river clean, so I am fairly sure that is most of what they want. Then further out there is the water, and the fish in it, which count for less here than the people do and still count. And further out still there are the towns, which want water nobody has to drive to.

The closing can be undone, which is most of what it has going for it. Nobody has to decide it in December. If the office opens again in March and people have stopped coming, that can be mended, and people can start again next year. So when it is only a question of finding out who can do this work, I would ask, and I would not guess. The note gives you one thing. It mentions Rachel McGuire, and it mentions her alone. Whether there is a staff member whose job is volunteers, I do not know, and I would expect this note to tell you the same.

What is up to you is smaller than the note suggests, though smaller is still something. You can still be there on January 3. You can still keep a river clean, because that is in your hands whatever the office does. And you can still take the lead. If there is more in your hands than either of us expects, I would still want the step that can be undone.

The note also says it is time to recertify. I would want to know what that asks of people.

Here is the note as you described it.

Dedicate yourself to the water. You cannot make this office's decisions for it, and you do not have to. You can still be there on January 3, and you can still keep a river clean.

Here is one that closes the gap instead.

The gap is open, and something is missing. The office closes on December 20 and re-opens on January 3, and nobody has told anyone who picks up for it. Before December 20, find out from the office whether anyone covers for it while it is away. If nobody does, write it down today, with the dates, to the people who answer for it. The volunteers are the ones it lands on, and they are the nearest people in this who did not get a say. I am fairly sure it falls on them. I do not know how much a volunteer would want from this, so I would ask before I wrote it down.

The line above is mine, and people who think hard about volunteers land in odd places across it. Some would say that an office which closes for the holidays and re-opens on schedule has already shown them what it wants, and that asking would only mean pushing. Some would say that the people who answer for it know things about the budget that nobody else does. I lean slightly ahead of the middle on this. I would still think that asking costs a volunteer very little. I am less sure that it costs anything at all. A lot of people who write about this would say that a volunteer who pushes hard on his own reading of what the people around him want is the very thing nobody can check. The gap is about as narrow as a gap gets. Once someone has asked, it is gone. Nobody has to settle anything about anyone. And asking can be undone, because a question can be dropped, which is most of what it has going for it. If the office says no, the people who answer for it lose a few days, and the people further out still have their water.

The note is from the office itself, sent to the people who give their time to it, and that counts for more with me than any reading of it. I hold the lean loosely, though I hold it for a reason. If the office has closed for the holidays every year for as long as anyone has kept its records, I would think it wants this, and I would think so with moderate confidence, and the people further out still count for more with me than the office does. I would want it to say so in one line.

Here is the note as you described it.

The AWW Office closes on December 20, 2018, and re-opens on January 3, 2019. Before December 20, find out from the office whether anyone covers for it while it is away. If nobody does, write it down today, with the dates, to the people who answer for it. The office is the one here who did not get a say. It loses a few days, and it can put things right.

Here is one more, for people who would rather not ask.

It is time to recertify. The office closes for the holidays, and it comes back on schedule. The water comes back too. Find out what recertifying asks of you this year, and ask what it is like being the only one there.
